papers.what_it_is: A theoretical and perturbative-numerical argument, by mapping adiabatic quantum optimization of random Exact Cover 3 instances to the Anderson model on a hypercube, that minimum spectral gaps become smaller than exponentially small in N.

assertions.value: The authors define adiabatic quantum optimization with an interpolating Hamiltonian between an easy-to-prepare initial Hamiltonian and the problem Hamiltonian, with the parameter s increasing with time as s = t/T.
quotes: Hˆ (s) = (1 − s)Hˆ0 + sHˆP where s is a tunable parameter
increase s with time as s = t/T
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section b, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the adiabatic condition requires the run time T to scale as one over the square of the gap between the ground state and the first excited state, so that adiabatic quantum optimization is not efficient when the gap is small.
quotes: the adiabatic condition requires that T ∼
Therefore AQO is not eﬃcient when ∆ is small.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to the Adiabatic Theorem [6], not proved in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the adiabatic model has been shown to be equivalent to the standard circuit model of quantum computing.
quotes: This model has since been shown to be equivalent to the standard (circuit) model
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result [7], not shown in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the adiabatic quantum approach to NP-complete problems can beat known classical algorithms provided that the minimal value of the gap scales as an inverse power of the problem size N.
quotes: the adiabatic quantum approach to NP-complete problems can beat known classical algorithms (which require exponential time) provided that the minimal value of the gap scales as an inverse power of the problem size N
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without a proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors cite earlier work showing that the gap can become exponentially small under specific conditions, such as a bad choice of initial Hamiltonian, or for specifically designed hard instances.
quotes: the gap can become exponentially small under speciﬁc conditions, such as a bad choice of initial Hamiltonian [8, 9]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work [8, 9].

assertions.value: The authors cite earlier work arguing that the presence of a first order phase transition could induce an exponentially small gap, demonstrated for a particular instance of an NP-hard problem and later for planted instances of 3-SAT.
quotes: it was recently argued that the presence of a ﬁrst order phase transition could induce an exponentially small gap
and later for planted instances of 3-SAT
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work [13, 14].

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier numerical simulations found the minimum gap for random instances to seem to decrease only polynomially for small instances, up to N = 124 for the latest simulations.
quotes: numerical simulations [5, 15, 16] where the minimum gap seemed to decrease only polynomially for small instances, up to N = 124 for the latest simulations [17]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work [5, 15, 16, 17].

assertions.value: The authors state that, as N goes to infinity, the typical value of the minimal gap for random instances decays even faster than exponentially.
quotes: the typical value of the minimal gap for random instances decays even faster than exponentially
assertions.certainty_reason: The result rests on a perturbative argument with stated approximations, not a rigorous proof; the authors write that the findings 'suggest' it.
assertions.reader_inference: The derivation (Sections g to i) uses perturbation theory and the cluster expansion with a stated 'estimate', not a theorem with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as a result of the decay of the minimal gap, the probability for adiabatic quantum optimization to yield a wrong solution in the large N limit tends to unity.
quotes: the probability for AQO to yield a wrong solution in this limit tends to unity
assertions.certainty_reason: A consequence of the perturbative gap estimate, not a rigorous proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that adiabatic quantum optimization fails for large random instances of NP-complete problems because the system gets trapped in one of the numerous local minima.
quotes: This implies that unfortunately, adiabatic quantum optimization fails: the system gets trapped in one of the numerous local minima.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion resting on the perturbative argument, stated as an implication of it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the appearance of exponentially small spectral gaps can be naturally attributed to Anderson localization of the eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian in the space of the solutions.
quotes: The appearance of exponentially small spectral gaps can be naturally attributed to the Anderson localization (AL) of the eigenfunctions of Hˆ (s) in the space of the solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement; the supporting argument is given in later sections.

assertions.value: The authors cite the Wigner-von Neumann non-crossing rule: the curves that describe the dependence of two eigenenergies on s do not cross, unless there is a special symmetry reason.
quotes: the curves that describe the s-dependence of two eigenenergies do not cross on the (E, s)-plane
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to von Neumann and Wigner [18].

assertions.value: The authors state that, in a reduced two-level model, the minimal value of the energy gap is determined by the off-diagonal matrix element, which is exponentially small under Anderson localization conditions.
quotes: The minimal value of the energy gap is determined by the oﬀ-diagonal matrix element i.e., ∆min = |V12| which is exponentially small under AL conditions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement from a two-level reduction; the exponential smallness is argued, not proved, in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors define an Exact Cover 3 clause as satisfied if and only if one of its three bits is 1 and the other two are 0, and a solution as an assignment of the bits that satisfies all of the clauses.
quotes: each clause is said to be satisﬁed if and only if one of the corresponding bits is 1 and the other two are 0
A solution of a particular instance of EC3 is an assignment of the bits x = (x1, x2, . . . , xN ) which satisﬁes all of the clauses.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines EC3 in Section d, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors assign the problem a cost function in which each solution has zero cost and all other assignments have a positive cost.
quotes: each solution has zero cost and all other assignments have a positive cost
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the cost function in Section d, p.4.

assertions.value: The authors pick one NP-complete problem, Exact Cover 3, the same problem used for the early numerical simulations of adiabatic quantum optimization, to explain the connection to Anderson localization.
quotes: we pick a particular NP-complete problem known as Exact Cover 3 (EC3), the same problem that was used for the early numerical simulations of AQO
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the problem its analysis covers in Section d, p.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The analytic result is derived for EC3 only; extension to other problems is a belief (next assertion).

assertions.value: The authors state that they believe the analysis can be extended to any NP-complete problem, and that the methods can be applied to other similar problems such as 3-SAT.
